sources.title: Massimo Vidale and Roberto Micheli: Protohistoric graveyards of the Swat Valley, new light on funerary practices and absolute chronology
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Antiquity study used for revised chronology, secondary burial, perishables, and prolonged interaction between living communities and graves.

sources.title: University of Padua research record: Excavations at the Protohistoric Graveyards of Gogdara and Udegram
sources.note: University catalogue for the full excavation monograph, used for scope, sites, grave architecture, reopening, body-part rearrangement, and publication context.

sources.title: Vidale, Micheli, and Olivieri: Excavations at the Protohistoric Graveyards of Gogdara and Udegram
sources.note: Full university-repository excavation monograph used for structures, multiple deposition episodes, grave reopening, perishable containers, and cautious ritual interpretation.

sources.title: Narasimhan et al.: Formation of Human Populations in South and Central Asia, supplementary materials
sources.note: Harvard-hosted Science supplement used for the preferred Swat Protohistoric Graves label, Udegram and Gogdara phases, sample context, and chronology.

sources.title: Narasimhan et al.: The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed ancient-DNA study used to explain multiple ancestry clines, steppe-related ancestry in the region, and why genetics cannot identify language or ethnicity.

sources.title: Luca Maria Olivieri: The Archaeology of Gandhara
sources.note: Oxford Research Encyclopedia chapter used for the northern Gandhara graveyard horizon, its approximate 1200 to 900 BCE setting, iron, and separation from later urban Gandhara.

sources.title: The chronology of Barikot: a reassessment of the stratigraphic sequence
sources.note: Peer-reviewed chronology used for the 1200 to 800 BCE transition and the much later early-historic urban phase beginning around 500 BCE.

sources.title: Agricultural strategies at Barikot in the Swat Valley from the late second millennium BCE onward
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeobotanical study used cautiously for settlement scale, crops, seasonal farming, irrigation implications, and its long multi-period sampling limits.

sources.title: Ca’ Foscari University Khyber Path project: Barikot site
sources.note: Official university excavation-project page used for Barikot landscape and site context and for the limits of published domestic water and sanitation evidence.

sources.title: Los Angeles County Museum of Art: Cremation Urn with Lid
sources.note: Official museum record used for a circa 1200 BCE Swat Valley earthenware urn attributed to the Gandhara Grave Culture, with provenance limitations kept explicit.

sources.title: University of Peshawar: Ancient Pakistan, Volume III
sources.note: Official journal contents page used to document the original Timargarha cemetery reports, skeleton study, pottery, small finds, and Balambat settlement publication.

sources.title: Indian Archaeology Today: Gandhara Grave Culture synthesis
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis used for pins, needles, ornaments, stitched-clothing clues, and the poorly known settlement and house plans, with older interpretations treated cautiously.

sources.title: Essays in Indian Protohistory: Gandhara Grave Culture material evidence
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis used for pottery, spindle whorls, bone tools, weapons, beads, metal objects, and sparse iron-bearing graves.

sources.title: Elisa Iori: Swat protohistory and the archaeology of Barikot and Balambat
sources.note: University of Bologna dissertation used for settlement-sequence context and caution against merging cemetery phases with later domestic architecture.

sources.title: A Protohistoric Grave from Aligrama, Swat: funerary goods and chronological implications
sources.note: Published grave study used for one securely contextualized assemblage containing iron objects, a chlorite vessel, pottery, and a spindle whorl.

sources.title: Archaeology Magazine: Burials and Reburials in Ancient Pakistan
sources.note: Reputable archaeological report used for Udegram reburials and textile-working clues including pins, ivory spindles, and chlorite whorls.

sources.title: Journal of Asian Civilizations: Burial variability in the Gandhara Grave Culture
sources.note: University journal survey used for variation in body placement, inhumation, cremation, fractional burial, and grave structures across cemeteries.

sources.title: Antiquity Project Gallery: Archaeological investigations in Chitral
sources.note: Antiquity project report used to show that similar-looking Chitral burials have their own long scientifically dated sequence and cannot be merged automatically with Swat.

sources.title: Muhammad Zahir: The Gandhara Grave Culture, new perspectives on chronology and identity
sources.note: Specialist review used for historiography, disputed dating, cremation and inhumation, and rejection of simple ethnic or Vedic equations.

sources.title: Muhammad Zahir: The Protohistoric Cemeteries of Northwestern Pakistan, deconstruction and reinterpretation
sources.note: University thesis used for the overview and its central warning that Gandhara Grave Culture is a modern analytical category, not a self-named people.

sources.title: University of Washington: British Library Kharoṣṭhī Fragments
sources.note: University resource used to date surviving Gandhari written material centuries later and to justify providing no falsely contemporaneous written-language sample.

proposedOverrides.summary: The atlas ends this archaeological culture at 700 BCE, but revised site chronologies vary and no single historical fall event is known.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed id is gandhara-grave-culture, displayed Gandhara grave culture, classified as a circa culture from 1000 to 700 BCE.
It was initially missing a researched card and override; coverage recorded one border file and one observed interval, 1000 to 700 BCE.
The exact target is absent at 1500 BCE, appears once at 1000 BCE, and is absent at the indexed 700 BCE endpoint and later 500 and 300 BCE seams.
The 1000 BCE feature is one Polygon with one part, one ring, and nine positions; bounds are [68.96408964089642,32.00097861956844,74.22014220142202,35.11707656170631].
Its raw coordinate SHA-256 is 1b32fc4516879de309c7a90d01c660b1edd60fa0d49683a64b9bcd22a94c55bd; canonical hash is 6a9eb0f94aa3c9cb803591f598fe307f315a61482274a158244f30bfbcb37013.

The polygon includes tested points at Loebanr III, Butkara II, Katelai, Aligrama, Udegram, Barikot, Timargarha, Peshawar, Charsadda, and Taxila but excludes the tested Dir point, Chitral, Kabul, Gilgit, Srinagar, Harappa, and Mehrgarh.
Its breadth beyond middle Swat and exclusion of the tested Dir point show that it is a coarse imported footprint, not a surveyed archaeological distribution.
The predecessor dravidians and endpoint vedic-aryans owners are atlas display categories and are not evidence of language, ethnicity, or population replacement.
The later gandhara id at 500 BCE is a distinct political-geographic record and must not be treated as the same entity as the grave-culture label.
Gandhara Grave Culture is a modern archaeological grouping; the card prefers Swat Protohistoric Graves where useful and does not infer a self-name, language, or single ethnicity.
No contemporaneous inscription or manuscript is securely tied to the target; later Gandhari and Kharoṣṭhī evidence is explicitly excluded as a writing sample.
